title: How Languages Work
summary: The toolkit behind every language map: sounds, words, word order, writing systems and how adults actually acquire a language. Its threshold is the idea that every human language is fully rule-governed and expressive; the differences are in where the complexity sits.
sources: Ladefoged & Johnson: A Course in Phonetics
Krashen: Principles and Practice in Second Language Acquisition (1982)
Nation: Learning Vocabulary in Another Language
WALS: The World Atlas of Language Structures (Dryer & Haspelmath)

nodes.label: Phonetics & the IPA
nodes.summary: One symbol per sound, for every language: the International Phonetic Alphabet.
nodes.outcome: Transcribe a short word in the IPA.
nodes.check: Why do linguists use the IPA instead of ordinary spelling?
nodes.answer: Spelling is inconsistent within and across languages; the IPA gives one symbol per sound.

nodes.label: Phonemes & Minimal Pairs
nodes.summary: Sounds that change meaning in a language; what counts as 'different' varies by language.
nodes.outcome: Find minimal pairs that prove two sounds are separate phonemes.
nodes.check: 'Ship' and 'sheep' differ by one sound. What is such a pair called?

nodes.label: Tone
nodes.summary: In tonal languages, pitch contour distinguishes words.
nodes.outcome: Explain how tone distinguishes words in Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai or Yoruba.
nodes.check: In Mandarin, what changes when you change the pitch contour of 'ma'?
nodes.answer: The meaning: mā (mother), má (hemp), mǎ (horse) and mà (scold) are different words.

nodes.label: Morphology: How Words Are Built
nodes.summary: Roots, prefixes and suffixes; isolating, agglutinative and fusional languages.
nodes.outcome: Segment words into morphemes and classify a language's morphology.

nodes.label: Word Order & Syntax
nodes.summary: SVO, SOV, VSO and the patterns that travel with them (prepositions vs postpositions).
nodes.outcome: Predict other word-order features from a language's basic order.
nodes.check: English is SVO. What is the basic word order of Japanese, Korean, Hindi and Turkish?

nodes.label: "Some languages are primitive"
nodes.summary: Every natural language is fully expressive and rule-governed; complexity moves between sounds, words and syntax.
nodes.outcome: Refute the idea of primitive languages with examples.
nodes.check: Are there 'primitive' human languages with simpler, less complete grammar?
nodes.answer: No: every natural human language is fully expressive and rule-governed; complexity just sits in different places.

nodes.label: Language Families
nodes.summary: Languages descend from common ancestors; sound correspondences, not look-alike words, prove relationship. Once this lands, vocabulary across a family becomes predictable.
nodes.outcome: Place a language in its family and branch.
nodes.check: Hindi, Persian, Russian, Spanish and English all belong to which language family?

nodes.label: Writing Systems
nodes.summary: Alphabets, abjads, abugidas, syllabaries and logographies.
nodes.outcome: Classify a script and say what it writes.
nodes.check: What is the difference between an alphabet and an abjad?
nodes.answer: An alphabet writes consonants and vowels; an abjad (like Arabic or Hebrew) mainly writes consonants, leaving vowels implied.

nodes.label: Pragmatics & Politeness
nodes.summary: Meaning in context: indirect requests, honorifics and register.
nodes.outcome: Choose the right register for a situation in another language.
nodes.check: Why is answering 'Can you pass the salt?' with 'Yes' (and not passing it) a joke?
nodes.answer: It is an indirect request, not a question about ability: meaning depends on context (pragmatics).

nodes.label: Second-Language Acquisition
nodes.summary: Comprehensible input, output and interaction; explicit grammar helps but doesn't replace use.
nodes.outcome: Design a week of study that balances input, output and review.
nodes.check: What does Krashen's comprehensible-input hypothesis claim?
nodes.answer: We acquire language by understanding messages slightly beyond our current level (i + 1).

nodes.label: "Adults can't really learn a new language"
nodes.summary: Adults often learn faster at first; a native-like accent is harder after childhood, but high proficiency is very achievable.
nodes.outcome: Set realistic goals for adult learners.
nodes.check: Can adults learn a second language to a high level?
nodes.answer: Yes: adults often progress faster at first; a native accent is harder, but high proficiency is very achievable.

nodes.label: Vocabulary & Spaced Repetition
nodes.summary: A few thousand frequent words carry most text; spaced retrieval makes them stick.
nodes.outcome: Build a frequency-ordered, spaced vocabulary plan.
nodes.check: Roughly how many of the most frequent word families cover the large majority of everyday text?

nodes.label: "Similar-looking words mean the same thing"
nodes.summary: False friends look alike across languages but mean different things.
nodes.outcome: Spot common false friends between English and a target language.
nodes.answer: Pregnant, not embarrassed: a false friend.
